claims.claim: Enabling commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits turns a single expired or rotated signing key into a fleet-wide outage with no owning signal: the hydrator design delegates every push to the commit server, so when the commit server fails at startup on a missing/invalid key it stops new hydrated commits for every hydrator-enabled app, and the only detection path is a generic CrashLoopBackOff on whoever holds pod-health paging, who then has to find someone with access to the signing-key Secret before anything can be fixed.

Turning on hydrated-commit signing is precisely what breaks the rollback path: once the operator adds the public key to the project's SourceIntegrity policy, the History and Rollback push, which happens outside the commit server and therefore lands unsigned, is rejected by the git host, and the UI surfaces only a failed push with no message tying it to signing and no retry, so the rollback that ops relies on after a bad promotion fails at the moment it is needed and with no diagnosis attached.

With hydrator rollback deprioritized to next quarter and the dev pair moved onto the progressive sync deletion loop, the Reverse deletionOrder ships without any automated revert: Reverse waits for one Application to be fully deleted before moving to the next, and a child stuck Progressing means that wait never completes, leaving a half-deleted ApplicationSet whose recovery is entirely hand work by whoever is on at the time.

The spec-only RollingSync miss has no detection path at all: the ApplicationSet reports the rollout complete while children sit OutOfSync, controller logs at warn emit no progressive-sync transitions, and no counter increments when specChanged fires without a resulting sync operation, so the incidence is a count of support pings rather than a rate. The proposed progressive sync metrics do not close this: their four questions cover trigger latency, per-step duration, refresh counts, and what a stalled sync is waiting on, none of which fires when the controller believes the step already finished.

The only guard against the delete/recreate wave-restart loop is a runbook sentence telling operators to switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce before deleting a child app by hand, with no controller-level check or alert behind it, and the roadmap simultaneously commits to teardown remaining a manual operator action performed one Application at a time through interfaces that expose no deletion ordering. The manual per-app teardown the roadmap prescribes is the exact action that arms the loop, so the mitigation depends entirely on the operator remembering the note at the hour they are doing the deletion.

In push-to-stage mode the load-bearing component of the deploy path is an unowned shell script: the hydrator design explicitly relies on an external system to move changes from the stage branch to the deployment branch, the stage-branch promoter is still that shell script with nobody on it, and its lag is not merely slow but incorrect, because auto-sync will immediately apply whatever the stage branch last held, which can be very old manifests. There is no owner to page and no signal that distinguishes a stalled promoter from a quiet one.

The CI diff failure and its root cause never meet in a place an operator will look: the ticket's error text names system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server and the reporter concludes the broad cluster Secret should have covered it, while the actual mechanism, that with impersonation enabled the diff runs as the destination service account which lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources, exists only in a platform sync call note that says someone should write it onto the ticket. Every future report of this error re-runs the same wrong investigation into cluster credentials until that note is transcribed.

The impersonation feature's least-privilege posture carries a permanent, unbudgeted maintenance tax because the diff path was never decoupled with the sync path: sync honors destinationServiceAccounts, Server-Side Diff runs as the cluster Secret credential and needs real patch authority on every resource kind in the Application, so each new chart kind produces a ComparisonError and forces another patch rule onto the standing cluster role, five rounds so far with no end state. Detection is the App rotating Synced and Unknown on every reconcile, and the remediation is always widening the very credential the impersonation design set out to narrow.

Parallel progressive sync steps would raise concurrent reconcile load against multiple cluster groups at once while QPS and Burst remain a single global setting applied to all managed destination clusters, so the operator must pick one rate for the strongest and weakest cluster simultaneously. The failure lands on the under-provisioned edge cluster as API server throttling, elevated latency, or an API server crash, which surfaces on the target cluster's own monitoring rather than as any Argo CD signal, so the team that gets woken is not the team that shipped the parallel rollout.

The incident review's interim rule that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists, because every hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave, is an unenforced convention living in a review note that has not yet been written onto the pilot ticket, while an open request asks for Source Hydrator support in ApplicationSets specifically to control destroy ordering of generated Applications. Building that would make the banned combination the intended configuration, and nothing in the controller would stop a team from adopting it; the first detection is the wave-restart loop itself.
